pains.title: Profit on paper, no cash on payroll day
pains.problem: Technicians are paid every two weeks, but Medicaid can take 30 to 90 days to pay. Every new client uses cash before it produces any.
pains.how: Lucid shows profit and cash side by side in a rolling forecast with payer mix tracking. Lucid works alongside your biller and does not chase claims.

pains.title: Paid hours versus billed hours, authorized versus delivered
pains.problem: RBTs are paid for all hours worked, but revenue comes only from billed units. Drive time and paid cancellations have no claim behind them.
pains.how: Lucid tracks authorized against delivered hours and shows margin by location and by provider. Scheduling and authorizations stay with your team.

pains.title: State rate cuts and one payer too big
pains.problem: Each state sets its own Medicaid rates and caps. Indiana cut maximum fees for individual (nongroup) ABA services by 6 percent from April 2026, according to ABA provider groups.
pains.how: Lucid builds your books by payer and runs rate cut and hour cap scenarios in your forecast. Lucid does not negotiate rates.

faq.q: Why does my ABA practice show a profit but I am short on cash for payroll?
faq.a: Your books count a session as revenue the day it is delivered, but Medicaid can take 30 to 90 days to pay and other payers often a month or more, while technicians are paid every two weeks. Growth makes the gap bigger. Lucid's cash flow forecast, with payer mix tracking, shows a shortfall weeks ahead.

faq.q: How do I know how much revenue I am losing when clients get fewer hours than approved?
faq.a: Compare authorized hours per week with billed hours per week, client by client, and price the difference at your rate. Lucid tracks authorized against delivered hours, so the leak becomes a dollar figure.

faq.q: What does it really cost my ABA practice every time an RBT quits?
faq.a: It includes recruiting, paid training, weeks of hours you cannot bill and sometimes a lost client, and estimates vary a lot. Lucid's CFO scenario planning can test whether a raise or guaranteed hours pays for itself.

faq.q: Can I pay my RBTs as 1099 contractors to save on payroll taxes?
faq.a: Most guidance in the ABA field says RBTs work under close direction and should be treated as employees, and getting this wrong can mean back taxes and penalties. Lucid's classification review flags issues, but ask an employment attorney for the final call.

faq.q: Is it more profitable to run in-home ABA or open a center?
faq.a: Neither is always better. In-home loses margin to drive time and cancellations, and a center loses it to rent when rooms sit empty. Lucid splits your numbers by setting and location so you see which one earns its keep before you sign another lease.
